stimulus.description: Demand schedule faced by a single seller (a monopolist) with constant marginal cost and average total cost equal to $30 per unit.

notes: Marginal cost = average total cost = $30 per unit.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: The firm maximizes profit. Calculate the profit-maximizing quantity and the price the firm charges. Show your work.

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost (MR = 60 - 2Q) and solves for the quantity (answer 15)
common_errors: sets P = MC and gets the competitive quantity 30

rubric_rows.criterion: Reads the price from the demand curve at the profit-maximizing quantity (answer $45)
common_errors: uses MR instead of P at that quantity

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the firm's economic profit.

rubric_rows.criterion: Profit = (P - ATC) x Q (answer)
common_errors: uses MC instead of ATC for the margin

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the deadweight loss caused by the monopoly relative to the efficient quantity (where P = MC).

rubric_rows.criterion: Computes the triangle with base Q_efficient - Q_monopoly and height P - MC (answer)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Suppose marginal cost rises by $10 per unit (and demand is unchanged). Does the profit-maximizing quantity increase, decrease, or stay the same? Explain.
parts.model_answer: Quantity decreases: MR = MC now occurs at Q = 10 < 15 because higher marginal cost intersects the same MR curve at a smaller quantity.

rubric_rows.criterion: States quantity decreases and links the higher MC to the MR = MC intersection at a smaller quantity
alt_solutions: marginal cost curve shifts up and meets marginal revenue at a lower quantity
common_errors: says quantity is unchanged because demand is unchanged

ap_microeconomics-f02.title: Oligopoly game: dominant strategies and equilibrium

stimulus.description: Payoff matrix for two firms, Firm A (rows) and Firm B (columns), each choosing to not advertise or advertise. The firms choose simultaneously, once, with no binding agreement. Payoffs are profits in millions of dollars, listed as (Firm A, Firm B).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Does Firm A have a dominant strategy? If so, identify it and justify using the payoffs.
parts.model_answer: Yes: advertise. If Firm B chooses not advertise, Firm A earns 83 vs 67; if Firm B chooses advertise, Firm A earns 44 vs 32; so advertise is better regardless.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the dominant strategy
common_errors: says there is no dominant strategy

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by comparing payoffs against each of the rival's choices (uses the payoff numbers)
alt_solutions: better regardless of what the other firm does

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Identify the Nash equilibrium of the game.
parts.model_answer: (Firm A: advertise, Firm B: advertise).

rubric_rows.criterion: States the equilibrium strategy pair for both firms

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: What are the payoffs of Firm A and Firm B in the Nash equilibrium?
parts.model_answer: $44 million for Firm A and $44 million for Firm B.

rubric_rows.criterion: Reads both equilibrium payoffs (answer)

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Both firms would earn more if they both chose not advertise/not advertise. Explain why they might not reach that outcome without an enforceable agreement.
parts.model_answer: Each firm has an incentive to deviate to its dominant strategy (it earns more whatever the rival does), so the cooperative outcome is not stable without enforcement.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains the incentive to deviate (dominant strategy) makes the cooperative outcome unstable
alt_solutions: each firm does better by choosing the dominant strategy
common_errors: says the cooperative outcome is not feasible because payoffs are lower
